wine.name: Tom Cullity Cabernet Sauvignon Malbec
wine.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, the great majority, with Malbec for most of the rest; a little Petit Verdot joined some of the early vintages.
wine.sites: The Home Vineyard at Wilyabrup, planted by the founder in 1967: old, dry grown Cabernet of the Houghton clone on its own roots, in deep gravel loam over clay beside the Wilyabrup Brook.
wine.making: Whole berries are fermented with wild yeast, the Cabernet in closed static fermenters and the Malbec in open ones, and the wine stays from under two weeks to a month on its skins. It is then aged for about eighteen months in French oak barriques, the larger part of them new, before bottling.
wine.glass: Blackberry, cassis and ripe plum over liquorice, dark chocolate and a smoky, savoury note of nori; full yet poised, with fine, firm tannin and fresh acidity.
wine.ageing: Closed and firm for its first five years or so, it opens over the following decade and is made to keep for twenty years and more in a strong vintage.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle for an hour or two, an old one gently off its sediment; a Bordeaux glass.

label.means: The founder's name, given to the house's leading red from the 2013 vintage.
Australian law lists the grapes of a blend in descending order, so Cabernet is the larger share.
The Geographical Indication: at least 85 per cent of the fruit must come from it.

records.table: Tom Cullity is the leading red of Vasse Felix, the region's first commercial vineyard, and bears the name of the doctor who planted it in 1967. Cabernet Sauvignon with Malbec from his own old vines, it is dark, firm and long, so give it air.
records.story: Dr Tom Cullity (1925 to 2008), a Perth heart specialist, took up the climate research of the mid 1960s that likened the cape to Bordeaux and went looking for land. In 1967 he planted a small vineyard at Wilyabrup, the first commercial vineyard of Margaret River, with Cabernet Sauvignon and Malbec among the first vines, and called it Vasse Felix. In 1972 he made a Cabernet Sauvignon Malbec and a Riesling, which the house counts as the region's first serious wines. Cullity sold the estate in the mid 1980s, and in 1987 the Holmes à Court family bought it. For years the house's leading red was the Heytesbury, a Cabernet led blend. To mark fifty years since the first planting, the house released in 2017 the 2013 vintage of a new flagship, named for the founder and grown on his old vines in the Home Vineyard, with Malbec in the blend as it had been in 1972. Tom Cullity took the Heytesbury red's place at the head of the range. For a sommelier it is the region's beginning in one bottle: the first vineyard, the first grapes and the man who planted them, poured as a wine for the cellar.

others.name: Heytesbury
others.note: The Cabernet led blend that was the house's leading red until Tom Cullity took its place.

others.name: Heytesbury Chardonnay
others.note: Taut, barrel worked Margaret River Chardonnay of grapefruit and struck flint.

traps: Tom Cullity is Cabernet Sauvignon with Malbec, not a straight Cabernet; Malbec has been in the house's red since its first of 1972.
The vines date from 1967 but the wine does not: the first Tom Cullity is the 2013 vintage, released in 2017.
Vasse Felix is in Margaret River in Western Australia, a long way from every South Australian region.

cards.front: Vasse Felix: which red bears the founder's name, and what is its first vintage?
cards.back: Tom Cullity, a Cabernet Sauvignon with Malbec; the 2013, released in 2017 for the estate's fiftieth year.

cards.front: Which estate planted the first commercial vineyard of Margaret River, at Wilyabrup in 1967?
cards.back: Vasse Felix, planted by Dr Tom Cullity, a Perth heart specialist.

questions.q: Which grape does the Tom Cullity of Vasse Felix blend with its Cabernet Sauvignon?
questions.exp: Malbec has partnered Cabernet in the house's red since 1972 and gives the second name on the label; Merlot, the usual partner in Bordeaux, plays no part.

questions.q: In which year did Dr Tom Cullity plant the vineyard of Vasse Felix at Wilyabrup?
questions.exp: Cullity planted in 1967, the region's first commercial vineyard; 1971 is when the Cullens planted their vineyard nearby, and 1972 the year of his first wines.

report: The founder's dates rest on the house's own history pages (1925 to 2008, a cardiologist), with his birth on 10 September 1925 confirmed by the State Library of South Australia; two further searches found no obituary or second source for the year of death, so 2008 stands on the house's page alone and the refuter may wish to try a newspaper archive.

The making rests on the importer Winebow's sheets of 2019 and 2021, a sheet of 2022 and The Real Review: wild yeast, whole berries, about eighteen months in French barriques with a new share from about half to four fifths by vintage, so the record says the larger part.

The first vintage of 2013 released in 2017, and Tom Cullity taking the Heytesbury red's place, rest on Decanter and The Buyer; the house's own story page has the founder hand the estate on in 1984 (to a couple, living or not, left unnamed) and another account gives a sale of 1985, so the story says the mid 1980s; the Holmes à Court purchase of 1987 rests on the house's page and a second profile.

Wikipedia says the first harvest of 1971 was lost to birds and bunch rot, and a mirror of it explains the name as a lucky or happy Vasse; neither found a second source, so both are left out, and say is empty for want of a source on how the house says its name.

The library's Heytesbury line calls it the long standing Cabernet blend of the house; Decanter and The Buyer say Tom Cullity supplanted the Heytesbury red from the 2013 vintage, so the record tells it as the earlier leading red.
The Wikipedia entry and one profile place the first vineyard at Cowaramup; the house gives the Home Vineyard's locality as Wilyabrup, which the record follows.

The first commercial vineyard of the region rests on the house's pages and Wikipedia; that the founder acted on the climate research of the mid 1960s rests on the library and the region record, not on a source read here, and the refuter may wish to try it.
Farmed organically was cut from sites: the house's organic farming is recent and not a habit of decades.

wine.name: Moss Wood Cabernet Sauvignon
wine.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, the great majority, with small amounts of Cabernet Franc and Petit Verdot.
wine.sites: The Moss Wood vineyard at Wilyabrup, first planted in 1969: unirrigated vines on gentle slopes facing north and east.
wine.making: Fermented in small open fermenters, the cap of skins plunged by hand several times a day. Each batch then rests apart in French oak barriques, a fifth or fewer of them new, for well over a year and a half before the blend is made, and the blend often goes back to barrel, so the wine has more than two years in oak in all.
wine.glass: Blackcurrant, plum and cherry over cedar, tobacco and bay leaf; medium to full in body, with bright acidity and fine, supple tannin, generous without losing its frame.
wine.ageing: Pleasant young, but made for the cellar: the house asks at least ten years, and a strong vintage reaches its height at twenty to twenty five.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle for an hour or so, an old one gently off its sediment; a Bordeaux glass.

label.means: The name of the vineyard and of the estate, planted at Wilyabrup in 1969.
A grape named alone on an Australian label must be at least 85 per cent of the wine.
The Geographical Indication of the cape in the south west of Western Australia.

records.table: Moss Wood Cabernet Sauvignon comes from the second vineyard of Margaret River, planted at Wilyabrup in 1969. Blackcurrant, plum and bay leaf over fine tannin, it spends two years and more in French oak and rewards a decade in the cellar.
records.story: A doctor and his wife bought land at Wilyabrup in 1969 and planted Cabernet Sauvignon there, the second commercial vineyard of the young region after Vasse Felix. The first wine came with the 1973 vintage, and the 1975 Cabernet carried the estate's name abroad: Decanter, from the winemaker's memory, tells it as the wine that first won notice beyond Australia for the cape's Cabernet. In 1979 the founders took on a winemaker and viticulturist, and in 1984 he and his wife leased the estate; by July 1985, as the house tells it, the sale was complete. The new owners later added the neighbouring Ribbon Vale vineyard and kept its wines under their own label, so Moss Wood Cabernet stays the wine of the vineyard of 1969. The house is patient with it: the Cabernet's batches are blended late, the wine has more than two years in barrel, and the house asks that it be cellared for a decade before it shows its full depth. For a sommelier it shows that Margaret River Cabernet can be generous and yet keep its shape for decades.

others.name: Moss Wood Ribbon Vale
others.note: Wines of a neighbouring Wilyabrup vineyard the house added later, kept under their own label.

others.name: Moss Wood Sémillon
others.note: Margaret River Sémillon, riper and fuller than the Hunter's.

traps: Moss Wood was planted in 1969, two years after Vasse Felix: it is the region's second vineyard, not its first.
Margaret River Sémillon such as Moss Wood's is riper and often fuller than the low alcohol Hunter Valley style.
Ribbon Vale wines come from a separate vineyard and are labelled apart; they are not the Moss Wood Cabernet.

cards.back: The 1975, which Decanter tells as the wine that first won the cape's Cabernet notice beyond Australia.

cards.front: Which Wilyabrup vineyard of 1969 was the second planted in Margaret River?
cards.back: Moss Wood, planted by a doctor and his wife; its Cabernet Sauvignon is the flagship.

questions.q: How long does Moss Wood usually age its Cabernet Sauvignon in barrel before bottling?
opts: Over two years in French barriques
questions.exp: The house gives the wine more than two years in French barriques, only a small share of them new, rather than American casks, old vats or a short spell in steel.

questions.q: Which vintage of Moss Wood Cabernet Sauvignon does the house single out as the one that made its name?
questions.exp: The 1975 is the vintage the house and Decanter single out; 1973 was the first vintage, 1969 the year of planting and 1985 the year of the sale.

report: The house's own pages give the founding couple of 1969, the winemaker's arrival in 1979, the lease of 1984 and the sale of July 1985, the pivotal 1975, the open fermenters, the twenty eight months in French barriques on average and the ageing advice; Langton's and Taste and Terroir agree on 1969, 1973 and the sale, with Langton's giving 1978 for the winemaker's arrival and 24 months in oak.
Living people kept out: the founding doctor and his wife, and the couple who bought the estate in 1985; whether the founder is living was not settled, so he is never named.
One profile calls Moss Wood the first winery to plant Cabernet Sauvignon in the region; Vasse Felix planted Cabernet in 1967 by its own account, so the claim is left out.

The library's holdings line (run since the 1980s) fits the sale of 1985, but the winemaker arrived in 1979; the 1973 first vintage made in a tin shed with a milk vat rests on one source and is left out.
The soil of the vineyard is not given: no source read named it, so sites keeps to the slopes and the dry farming.

The new oak share (15 to 20 per cent in the vintages of 2012, 2016, 2019 and 2021) and the late blending, with the blend often returned to barrel for its last months, rest on the house's vintage pages; the first draft's blended only at the end is corrected.

wine.name: Diana Madeline
wine.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, the great majority, with small amounts of Merlot, Cabernet Franc and Malbec.
wine.sites: The biodynamic Cullen Vineyard at Wilyabrup: Cabernet Sauvignon planted in 1971 on its own roots, Merlot and Cabernet Franc in 1976 and Malbec in 1978, dry farmed on gravelly sandy loam and granite over laterite.
wine.making: Picked by hand on the fruit and flower days of the biodynamic calendar and fermented with no yeast, acid or malolactic culture added, some lots staying for weeks on their skins. The wine is then aged for some thirteen to fifteen months in French barriques and puncheons, about half of them new.
wine.glass: Cassis, mulberry and plum over cedar, graphite and violet, with a note of iodine and ironstone; fine grained, chalky tannin and a long, cool finish.
wine.ageing: Supple enough to enjoy young, it holds for two decades and more, and the house claims as long as half a century for a strong vintage.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle for an hour or two, an old one gently off its sediment; a Bordeaux glass.

label.means: Named for the founder Diana Cullen; the wine was once labelled simply Cabernet Sauvignon Merlot.
The family name of the founders, Kevin and Diana Cullen, who planted the vineyard in 1971.
The Geographical Indication; Wilyabrup is a district within it, not a registered subregion.

records.table: Diana Madeline is the Cabernet blend of Cullen Wines, named for the founder who planted their Wilyabrup vineyard with her husband in 1971. Biodynamic, picked by the moon and mostly Cabernet Sauvignon, it is fine, cool and long.
records.story: Dr Kevin Cullen (1922 to 1994), a Busselton doctor remembered for founding the Busselton Health Study, and his wife Diana Cullen (1923 to 2003) ran sheep and cattle at Wilyabrup while raising six children. In the mid 1960s they thought of sowing lupins, and the lupin researcher they asked suggested vines instead. In 1966, with friends, they planted a small trial plot; as the family tells it, the young vines were sprayed with poison by mistake while the couple were away, and pulled out. In 1971 they planted again, on their own land, and the Cullen Vineyard grew from there, with Merlot and Cabernet Franc in 1976 and Malbec in 1978. Their daughter took charge of the winemaking in 1989, and the vineyard was certified biodynamic in 2004. The Cabernet blend, long labelled Cabernet Sauvignon Merlot, took the name Diana Madeline at the start of the 2000s in honour of its founder, and the Chardonnay became Kevin John, for her husband. For a sommelier the wine shows what the cape's Cabernet becomes when the farming leads and nothing is added in the cellar.

others.name: Kevin John
others.note: The Chardonnay named for the founder, wild fermented Wilyabrup Chardonnay, taut and long.

others.name: Mangan Vineyard
others.note: Wines of the family's second vineyard, beside the first, planted in 1995.

traps: Diana Madeline is Cabernet led: Merlot is only a small part, whatever the older Cabernet Sauvignon Merlot labels suggest.
Kevin John is the Chardonnay and Diana Madeline the red: each is named for one of the two founders.
The trial vines of 1966 were lost; the Cullen Vineyard dates from the planting of 1971.

questions.exp: The wine was long labelled Cabernet Sauvignon Merlot, though Merlot is a small part beside the Cabernet; Malbec is in the blend too but was never on the label, and Shiraz plays no part.

questions.exp: As the family tells it, the young vines were sprayed with poison by mistake while the couple were away; Vasse Felix, not the Cullens, made the region's first wines, and they planted again in 1971.

report: Kevin Cullen's dates (22 November 1922 to 9 February 1994) rest on the Australian Dictionary of Biography and Wikipedia; Diana Cullen's (1923 to 2003) on the Royal Agricultural Society of Western Australia and a Decanter report of her death at eighty. The society spells her second name Madeleine; the wine is Madeline.
The year the wine took the name Diana Madeline is the 2001 vintage by Decanter and the 2000 vintage by another account, so the record says the start of the 2000s.

Biodynamic certification is 2004 for the vineyard and 2008 for the winery on the house's pages and one importer's; another house page says certified since 2005, so the label line follows the more common reading.

The library's trap calls Wilyabrup a Margaret River subregion; the region record and the register know it only as an unofficial district (Margaret River has no registered subregion), so the record says a district.
Living people kept out: the founders' daughter, who has made the wine since 1989, and the lupin researcher who suggested vines, whose status was not settled.
The making follows the house's sheets of 2020 to 2024: thirteen to fifteen months in oak, forty to fifty five per cent new, barriques and puncheons, no added yeast, acid or malolactic culture.
The label's Biodynamic line was cut: no source read showed that the label prints the word, so the label keeps to the name, the house and the region.

wine.name: Art Series Chardonnay
wine.grapes: Chardonnay alone, of the Gingin clone, whose small berries carry slightly more sugar and acidity.
wine.sites: Estate blocks with northern aspects and rows running east to west; Block 20, by the front gate and planted in 1976, is the backbone, with Block 22 of 1978 beside it.
wine.making: Hand picked fruit is destemmed cool, given some skin contact, settled and fermented with cultured yeast in new French oak barriques, then aged on its lees, stirred often, for about eleven months. It is bottled after a light fining and released about three years after the vintage.
wine.glass: Grapefruit, lime curd and white nectarine over poached pear, then toasted hazelnut, cashew and a flinty edge; rich and layered, with taut acidity that carries a long finish.
wine.ageing: Tight on release despite its years at the estate; it gains nut and honey over a decade and keeps well beyond it in a strong vintage.
wine.serve: 10 to 13 degrees Celsius, not too cold; decant a young bottle briefly if it seems closed; a wide white Burgundy glass.

label.means: The estate's leading range, each label carrying a work by a contemporary Australian artist.
At least 85 per cent of the fruit comes from this Geographical Indication, here all estate grown.

records.table: Art Series Chardonnay is the white flagship of Leeuwin Estate, from a site a Napa vintner judged right for fine wine in 1972. Fermented and aged in new French oak and held about three years before release, it pairs grapefruit and cashew with taut acidity.
records.story: In 1972, as the house tells it, the Napa Valley vintner Robert Mondavi (1913 to 2008) visited the property and judged it right for fine wine; he went on to mentor its owners. The estate dates itself to 1973: a nursery went in in 1974, and from 1975 the vineyard blocks were planted by hand. Block 20, by the front gate, went in in 1976. The first commercial vintage was 1979, and in 1980 came the first Art Series Chardonnay, its label carrying a painting of Caves Road by a Western Australian artist, the start of a long line of labels carrying Australian paintings. Decanter in London singled out one of its first vintages, the 1980 or the 1981 by different accounts. The wine is fermented in new French oak, bottled some eighteen months after the vintage and released about three years after it, so a bottle on a list is older than most whites beside it. For a sommelier it is the Margaret River white a guest is likely to know by name.

others.name: Art Series Cabernet Sauvignon
others.note: The red of the same range, framed like Bordeaux and often overshadowed by the white.

others.name: Art Series Riesling
others.note: Dry Margaret River Riesling, a lighter regional counterpoint.

traps: Art Series is the name of a range with its own painted labels, not a single vineyard; the Chardonnay rests on Block 20.
The Art Series Chardonnay is released about three years after its vintage, so a current release is not a young wine.

questions.exp: The first Art Series Chardonnay is the 1980; 1972 is Mondavi's visit, 1974 the year the nursery went in, and the first commercial vintage was 1979.

report: founded keeps the library's 1974, the year the house's own story page gives for the nursery; the same page dates the estate itself to 1973 and Wikipedia agrees, while the media kit has the first vines planted later in 1972, so the library's year may want 1973.
Robert Mondavi's dates rest on the refuted napa record's Wikipedia source; his visit of 1972 rests on the house's media kit, Wikipedia and The Vintage Journal.
Blocks 20 and 22 and their years rest on Langton's and Berry Bros. and Rudd; the house's own pages read here name the Gingin clone and the north facing blocks but not the block numbers.

The first label painting, Caves Road, is the house's and The Vintage Journal's; its painter is not named because his dates were not confirmed in two sources, and the founders are living and not named.

The year of Decanter's recommendation is 1980 in the media kit and Wikipedia and 1981 on the house's story page and another account, so the story gives both; the open air concerts of the 1980s found no source and are left out.

The making follows the house's sheet of 2017 (cultured yeast, about eleven months in barrel) and two reviews giving all new French barriques; the release about three years after the vintage is the media kit's, and the bottling some eighteen months after it is one merchant's quotation of the house, read beside the 2019 sheet (bottled in August 2020).
Commissioned was cut from the label line and the story: the sources read say each label carries an Australian work of art, not whether each was commissioned or bought.

wine.name: Cape Mentelle Cabernet Sauvignon
wine.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, the great majority, with Petit Verdot and a little Merlot.
wine.sites: Estate vineyards that began with Wallcliffe, planted in 1970 on a ridge of free draining lateritic gravel from decomposed ironstone over gravelly clay; Trinders and other estate vineyards join it by vintage.
wine.making: Each batch is fermented apart, with wild and selected yeasts, and some stay on their skins for weeks after fermentation. The wine is then matured on its fine lees for about eighteen months in oak, chiefly French barriques, half or more of it new, before the blend is bottled.
wine.glass: Mulberry, blackcurrant and cassis with a leafy lift of fresh herbs, black olive, nori and liquorice; cocoa, cedar and violet come with age, over fine, sleek tannin.
wine.ageing: Firm and fruited young, it opens after about ten years, and the house gives a strong vintage twenty years and more.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle for an hour or two, an old one gently off its sediment; a Bordeaux glass.

label.means: A headland of the cape's coast, named by a French expedition of 1803 for a French geographer.
The Geographical Indication of the cape between Cape Naturaliste and Cape Leeuwin.

records.table: Cape Mentelle Cabernet Sauvignon took the Jimmy Watson Trophy, the Melbourne show's prize for a red a year old, in 1983 and again in 1984. From estate vineyards that began with Wallcliffe in 1970, it shows mulberry, cassis and black olive over fine tannin.
records.story: Three brothers founded Cape Mentelle in 1970 and named it for the nearby headland, which a French expedition had named in 1803 after a French geographer of the day. One of them, who had studied winemaking in California, made the wines. They planted the Wallcliffe Vineyard on lateritic gravel, adding Zinfandel in the early 1970s, a grape he had met in California, and the first Cape Mentelle wines came in the mid 1970s. In 1983 the 1982 Cabernet Sauvignon won the Jimmy Watson Trophy at the Royal Melbourne Wine Show, the award for a dry red a year old, and in 1984 the 1983 won it again: two wins in a row for a region whose first commercial vines went in only in 1967. The 1983 came from a hot, dry year, and the house says cool ocean breezes spared it the worst of the heat. In 1985 the founding winemaker went on to found Cloudy Bay in Marlborough, New Zealand. Veuve Clicquot took a stake in Cape Mentelle at the start of the 1990s and full ownership in 2000, and in 2023 it returned to Australian hands. For a sommelier the two trophies mark the years the cape's Cabernet won the notice of the whole country.

others.name: Cape Mentelle Zinfandel
others.note: From vines planted in the 1970s, a grape the founding winemaker met while studying in California.

others.name: Wallcliffe Sauvignon Blanc Semillon
others.note: The house's white blend of the two grapes, in its Wallcliffe range.

traps: The Jimmy Watson wins of 1983 and 1984 were for the 1982 and 1983 vintages: the trophy is judged on reds a year old.
Cape Mentelle's founding winemaker went on to found Cloudy Bay in Marlborough; the two houses are in different countries.
Cape Mentelle is named for a headland of the coast, not for a person of the house.

cards.back: The Jimmy Watson Trophy, for a dry red a year old, with the 1982 and the 1983 vintages.

questions.exp: The house describes free draining lateritic gravel from decomposed ironstone over gravelly clay; terra rossa over limestone is Coonawarra's soil, not Margaret River's.

questions.exp: The 1982 won in 1983 and the 1983 in 1984, since the trophy is judged on reds a year old; 1970 is the founding year and 2000 the year Veuve Clicquot took full ownership.

report: The house is not in the library: the founding of 1970 by three brothers, the trophies of 1983 and 1984 for the 1982 and 1983 vintages and the Veuve Clicquot purchase rest on the house's history page, Wikipedia and Decanter; the stake is 1990 and a half in two accounts and 1991 and seventy per cent in one, so the story says the start of the 1990s, with full ownership in 2000 in both.

The founding winemaker and his brothers are living or of unsettled status and are not named; his study in California is the house's (Fresno State) and Decanter's, and Cloudy Bay in 1985 is the house's newsletter with Decanter naming him its founder.

Edme Mentelle's dates were cut: the year of his death is 1815 in a Western Australian place name guide and 1816 in Wikidata and DBpedia, so the story describes him as a French geographer of the day; the naming of 1803 by the Baudin expedition rests on Wikipedia and that guide.

The first Cape Mentelle wine is dated 1976 in one house newsletter and 1974 in another, so the story says the mid 1970s; the Zinfandel planting is 1972 in one house source and 1974 in another, so the story says the early 1970s.

The house's own newsletter of 2023 announces its purchase by Paragon, and Decanter reported the sale by Moët Hennessy to an Australian group, so the story closes on the return to Australian hands in 2023 without naming the buyer.

The making and the sites rest on the house's sheets of 2016 and 2018: batches fermented apart, wild and selected yeasts, up to 35 and 65 days on skins, eighteen to twenty months on fine lees, about 55 per cent new oak in 2016 and four fifths in 2018, mostly French; the fruit came from Wallcliffe, Crossroads and Chapman Brook in 2016 and from Trinders and Wallcliffe in 2018, so sites no longer gives Wallcliffe alone.

The house also bottles a Heritage Cabernet Sauvignon from the old Wallcliffe vines alone, and its 2022 Cabernet Sauvignon draws on parcels across its vineyards with fourteen months in oak; the range has changed under its owners, so the checker may wish to confirm which bottling carries the line of the trophy wines.
